title: What if the polls are wrong again?
contentHtml:
It’s not unreasonable to approach election polls from a position of mild — maybe even more-than-mild — skepticism. In some cases this year, they’re projecting remarkable things, like Democrats having a chance to win a Senate seat in Kansas for the first time since 1932.

In the period that I’ve been covering politics, since 2008, remarkable things have happened, of course. America elected its first Black president. And then a reality-TV star was elected as his successor — and re-elected after a four-year hiatus after he’d twice been impeached. Republicans won a special Senate election in Massachusetts. Democrats won one in Alabama. Georgia became a swing state, while Ohio and Florida fell off the battleground map.

I argued earlier this week that what models like FLIPR are projecting for November isn’t necessarily all that bold. Yes, these forecasts predict a 10- or 11-point swing toward Democrats compared to the 2024 election. But the typical midterm swing is 7 or 8 points and the projected change isn’t any greater than in 2018, the previous Trump midterm — at which time, the president was considerably less unpopular than he is now and gas was much cheaper. The current state of the generic ballot is almost enough on its own to erase the large Republican advantage in states like Texas and Iowa where Democrats haven’t won in a long time. Pair that with some subpar Republican candidates, or unusually strong Democratic ones, and the math mostly checks out.

Still, and somewhat contrary to their reputation, models like FLIPR don’t just “trust the polls”. They adjust them in various ways and combine them with other sorts of evidence. The burden of proof is higher in states like Kansas where a Democratic win would represent more of a deviation. And they employ complex techniques to account for the possibility of polling error, including the chance that polls in the most important states all miss in the same direction.

To be honest — maybe this is an indication of the dark Republican mood — we haven’t actually seen all that much poll “unskewing” as compared to past cycles. I take the term from unskewedpolls.com, the 2012 website founded by a man named Dean Chambers, which basically just shifted every poll in Mitt Romney’s direction. But not only did Barack Obama win almost every swing state; he won them by more than polls predicted.

This is a bipartisan phenomenon, however. In 2024, some Democrats came up with elaborate justifications for why polls were underrating Joe Biden and Kamala Harris. But Trump beat his polling for the third presidential election in a row.

Where exactly is the line between hedging against the polls in various ways, as FLIPR does, and “unskewing” them? Welcome to the latest edition of “Nate’s tweets, explained,” which also doubles as a Model Talk:

This post on the Application Formerly Known as Twitter triggered a big reaction, with almost one million views as of this morning. As I said, I’ve been forecasting elections since FiveThirtyEight launched in 2008. I’ve been lucky in many ways, including that both 2008 and 2010 were almost freakishly accurate years for polling. This was always a bit ironic given that much of the purpose of a probabilistic model is to emphasize the uncertainty in the forecast.

Then in 2012, we got even luckier, with the FiveThirtyEight model “calling” every state correctly. But that counts Florida, where the odds were basically 50/50, and Obama only inched ahead in our forecast at the last minute. Our internal diagnostics gave us only a slim chance of getting a perfect score.

Another irony is that the polls weren’t all that great in 2012. Instead, they overestimated Romney and other Republicans by about 3 percentage points. Nobody that I can recall, except for former North Dakota Sen. Heidi Heitkamp1, has ever given me a hard time for this. Since all of our “calls” were right, nobody cared that some of the margins were a bit off.

Take a look at the final RealClearPolitics polling averages nationally in 2012, and in the 11 states they deemed “toss-ups.” Obama beat his national polls by 3 points. But this wasn’t really a matter of national polls being wrong and state polls being right. He also beat his state-by-state polling averages by around 3 points, with his final margins improving upon the RCP averages in all 11 states.2

(I’m not mentioning this to pick on RCP. They shouldn’t be confused with UnskewedPolls.com. After all, their averages had the right winner everywhere but Florida.3)

Polls missed low on Trump three times in a row

Since 2012, of course, there have been other systematic polling errors — but they usually haven’t been in Democrats’ favor. Instead, polls considerably underestimated Donald Trump and other Republicans on the ticket with him in 2016, 2020, and, to a slightly lesser extent, in 2024. (Irony #3: 2020 was actually the worst polling error of this trio, but the one election that Democrats won.)

To zoom out: In the 9 midterms or presidential years I’ve covered since FiveThirtyEight launched in 2008, polls have had a systematic bias against Democrats once, in 2012, a systematic bias against Republicans four times (the three Trump presidential elections + 2014), and were basically unbiased in the other four elections, including in the past two midterms.

What should you conclude from that? Well, maybe not much, because that’s hard to distinguish from random variation. Ignore, for now, the four elections where polls were basically unbiased. Where there were biases, they lowballed Democrats once and Republicans four times. But if you flip a fair coin 5 times, then 37.5 percent of the time, either heads or tails4 will come up at least 4 out of 5 times.

There’s also the fact that in elections during the Trump Era that didn’t coincide with a midterm or presidential election date, but particularly in 2025, polls have generally had a pro-R bias. This doesn’t get talked about much, but is more relevant than you might assume. It suggests that the recent pattern of anti-R bias becomes less consistent if you increase the sample size. And as I’ll get to later, it provides a hint about one possible explanation for why polls have been biased against Republicans when Trump himself was on the ballot, but not in other elections in the Trump Era.

Overall, the tendency for polls to underestimate Republicans in the Trump Era has been entirely concentrated on the three presidential election dates when Trump himself was on the ballot. These were big misses. If you take a simple average of every poll in the final three weeks of the campaign in our pollster ratings database from the 2016, 2020 and 2024 general elections, they overestimated Democrats by a margin of 3.8 percentage points.

However, polls in the previous two midterms in the Trump Era have been almost completely unbiased in the aggregate. And polls in the various off-year and special elections in the Trump years have been biased toward Republicans by an average of 1.3 points:

Silver Bulletin models account for the possibility of systematic polling errors

Before we go behind the paywall, I want to make several things abundantly clear to everyone:

  • FLIPR and other Silver Bulletin forecasts have always accounted for the possibility of correlated polling errors. These errors are fairly common — and they aren’t anything new. You should always be asking yourself questions like: what if Democrats or Republicans beat their polls everywhere by 3 points? Could they still win?

  • The mechanics of calculating these correlations are complicated, however. They’re where a lot of the work goes in when building an election model. For FLIPR, there are four layers of uncertainty incorporated into our simulations:

    • #1. The possibility of a uniform polling error in every race across the country, e.g., “Democrats beat their polls by 3 points across the board.”

    • #2. The possibility of demographically or geographically correlated polling errors, e.g. “Democrats beat their polls among Hispanics, but Republicans beat their polls in the Midwest.”

    • #3. The possibility of polling errors within one state, e.g. “Republicans beat their polls in both the Senate and gubernatorial races in Texas, and also in most of the House races there.”

    • #4. Finally, the possibility of a polling error that pertains to just one race, e.g. “Marie Gluesenkamp Perez beat her polls in Washington’s 3rd Congressional District”

  • As compared to presidential election years, midterm polling errors are somewhat less uniform, and FLIPR accounts for this. Much of the uncertainty in presidential elections is concentrated in the first layer — truly systematic errors that affect almost every state, like in 2012. For the midterms, they’re more evenly distributed between the four layers. In the past two midterms, 2018 and 2022, overall polling averages were largely unbiased, but there were significant regional errors.

  • Silver Bulletin models do not assume that any given poll or even the polling average in any given state is unbiased5:

    • At the individual poll level, our house effects adjustment evaluates systematic differences between polling firms in predicting the D versus R margin. Marist has typically had very good numbers for Democrats this cycle, for example. Maybe Marist is right. But FLIPR adjusts their polls to be closer to the consensus, as we do with any firm that shows these systematic differences.

    • And then at the race level, the polls are mixed with “fundamentals” and other adjustments. In the South Carolina Senate race, our polling average shows Republican Darline Graham ahead by only 2.6 points, for instance. But our forecast shows Graham winning by 5.3 after blending in fundamentals that account for how red South Carolina usually is.

Instead, the constraint we impose is that our forecast should be “party-neutral”. We expect Graham to outperform her current polling average in South Carolina because it’s a red state. But by the same measure, we expect Peggy Flanagan to outperform her polling average in Minnesota because it’s a blue state.

However, we don’t build in party-specific assumptions such as “polls always underestimate Republicans.” That’s what we’d consider to be “unskewing”. The polls have sometimes underestimated Republicans, and they might do that again this year. But we assume it’s roughly as likely that forecast errors benefit Democrats instead.

Let’s talk about why we think that’s the right assumption, and why we’re skeptical about people who confidently predict in which direction polls will be skewed.
